author: A Robot
objectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart, the four valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the ordered path of blood through pulmonary and systemic circulation using correct anatomical terminology.
Differentiate the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and relate the right and left sides of the heart to these circuits.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle.
Describe how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent backflow during different phases of the cardiac cycle.

modules.description: Students compare an intact exterior heart with a cutaway heart to establish anatomical orientation and patient-based right-left terminology.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the heart anatomically using apex position and great vessel placement.
Distinguish patient right and left from viewer right and left.
Relate external landmarks to internal cardiac anatomy.
instructions: Use Next and Previous to move through the guided scene.
Compare the intact heart on the left with the cutaway heart on the right.
Move around the tabletop workspace to inspect orientation from different angles.

components.text: Right and left are named from the patient's perspective.

clips.changeMeaning: Both heart models are rotated slightly to create a matched introductory view and help students see them as two representations of the same organ.
clips.narration: Welcome to the heart anatomy lab. You are viewing an intact exterior heart on the left and a cutaway heart on the right. Both are oriented anatomically, with the apex pointing downward and slightly to the patient's left.

clips.changeMeaning: The title updates and both hearts rotate toward a frontal perspective to support explanation of patient-based anatomical right and left.
clips.narration: Remember that anatomical right and left are described from the patient's perspective, not the viewer's. When you face the model, the right side of the heart appears on your left.

clips.changeMeaning: A vessel label appears and the exterior heart is tinted to direct attention to the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
clips.narration: On the exterior surface, note the major vessels: the superior and inferior vena cava, the pulmonary trunk and arteries, the pulmonary veins, and the aorta.

clips.changeMeaning: Attention shifts from the exterior model to the cutaway model so students can begin mapping outer form to internal chambers, septum, and valves.
clips.narration: The cutaway view reveals the four chambers, the septum, and the valves. Comparing the two views will help you connect external landmarks to internal structures and blood flow.

modules.description: A narrated structural tour highlights the chambers, valves, and major vessels in sequence while connecting internal and external anatomy.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers, four valves, and major vessels of the heart.
Locate each highlighted structure in a cutaway view and relate it to the intact heart.
Recognize that mitral and bicuspid are two names for the same valve.
instructions: Advance through each highlight in sequence.
Watch how the internal structure corresponds to a region on the exterior heart.
Pay special attention to valve names and positions.

clips.changeMeaning: The structural tour begins with chamber identification, and interior and exterior tags appear so students can compare both views simultaneously.
clips.narration: We begin with the four chambers of the heart. As each internal structure is discussed, use the intact heart to estimate its external position.

components.text: Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: The chamber list appears and the cutaway model is tinted to focus attention on the internal spaces of the heart.
clips.narration: The four chambers are the right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, and left ventricle. The atria receive blood, while the ventricles pump blood away from the heart.

components.text: Tricuspid, pulmonary, mitral or bicuspid, and aortic

clips.changeMeaning: The tour shifts from chambers to valves, with new text and color emphasizing one-way flow control structures inside the heart.
clips.narration: The four valves are the tricuspid valve, pulmonary valve, mitral or bicuspid valve, and aortic valve. Each valve helps keep blood moving in one direction.

components.text: Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Focus moves to the great vessels, and the exterior model is tinted because these structures are especially visible on the intact heart.
clips.narration: The major vessels include the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta. Notice which vessels enter the heart and which leave it.

components.text: Mitral valve and bicuspid valve are the same structure.

clips.changeMeaning: The cutaway heart enlarges slightly and the label isolates the mitral-bicuspid terminology note to reinforce a frequent naming point.
clips.narration: A final terminology note: the mitral valve and bicuspid valve are two names for the same left atrioventricular valve. You will see both terms in anatomy and clinical contexts.

modules.description: Color-coded blood pathways distinguish deoxygenated and oxygenated blood while introducing the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Associate blue with deoxygenated blood and red with oxygenated blood.
Differentiate the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit.
Explain the roles of the right and left sides of the heart in dual circulation.
instructions: Watch how blue and red regions correspond to blood oxygenation state.
Compare the pulmonary and systemic labels as the scene changes.
Note the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein naming pattern.

clips.changeMeaning: The scene introduces color coding and starts by emphasizing the pulmonary circuit with a blue label accent.
clips.narration: This scene introduces dual circulation using color. Blue represents deoxygenated blood, and red represents oxygenated blood.

components.text: Pulmonary circuit: right heart to lungs

clips.changeMeaning: The heart is tinted blue to emphasize the deoxygenated right-sided pathway and the pulmonary connection to the lungs.
clips.narration: The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood. Blood returns from the body, enters the right side, and is pumped to the lungs through the pulmonary arteries.

components.text: Systemic circuit: left heart to body

clips.changeMeaning: The heart tint shifts to red to emphasize the oxygenated left-sided pathway and the systemic outflow to the body.
clips.narration: The left side of the heart handles oxygenated blood. Blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins, enters the left side, and is pumped through the aorta to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Both circuit labels are simplified and the heart slightly enlarges to support side-by-side conceptual comparison of the two loops.
clips.narration: Together, the pulmonary and systemic circuits form one continuous dual-loop circulation. Remember the common exception: pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood, while pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: A single enlarged red blood cell is advanced stepwise through the complete circulation pathway, including gas exchange in the lungs.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the full path of blood through the heart and major vessels in order.
Identify where oxygenation occurs in the pulmonary circuit.
Relate forward movement of blood to chambers and valves.
instructions: Press Next to advance the red blood cell one step at a time.
Read the label at each location.
Replay the scene to practice the sequence until it becomes automatic.

components.text: Superior vena cava to right atrium

clips.changeMeaning: The blood cell enters the right atrium from the superior vena cava, beginning the deoxygenated return pathway.
clips.narration: A unit of deoxygenated blood returns from the body and enters the heart through the superior vena cava into the right atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: The blood cell moves through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, reinforcing the sequence from atrium to ventricle.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, moving the blood cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

components.text: Pulmonary valve to pulmonary trunk and arteries

clips.changeMeaning: The blood cell advances into pulmonary outflow, showing right ventricular ejection through the pulmonary valve.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts and pushes blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries on the way to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: At the lung capillaries, the blood cell changes from blue to red to mark oxygenation during gas exchange.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries, gas exchange occurs. The blood cell picks up oxygen and is now shown in red.

components.text: Pulmonary veins to left atrium through mitral region

clips.changeMeaning: The oxygenated blood cell returns from the lungs toward the left side of the heart, connecting pulmonary return to left atrial filling.
clips.narration: Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins, enters the left atrium, and approaches the mitral valve.

components.text: Left ventricle through aortic valve to aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The blood cell enters the left ventricle and is positioned for high-pressure ejection into the aorta.
clips.narration: The blood passes into the left ventricle. When the left ventricle contracts, it is pushed through the aortic valve into the aorta.

components.text: Systemic circulation and venous return to vena cava

clips.changeMeaning: The loop is completed as the blood cell travels through the body, loses oxygen, turns blue again, and returns in the veins.
clips.narration: The blood travels through systemic circulation, delivers oxygen to tissues, and returns deoxygenated through the veins to the vena cava, completing the loop.

modules.description: Side-by-side ventricular cross-sections compare myocardium thickness in the right and left ventricles and relate structure to function.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare right and left ventricular wall thickness visually and numerically.
Explain why the left ventricle requires a thicker myocardium.
Relate pressure demands to ventricular anatomy.
instructions: Compare the cross-sections on the left and right.
Watch the labels for approximate wall thickness values.
Use the comparison to connect form with circulatory workload.

clips.changeMeaning: Both cross-sections are color coded differently so the two ventricles can be compared immediately at the same cut level.
clips.narration: These cross-sections compare the right and left ventricles at the same horizontal level. Focus on the thickness of the muscular wall around each chamber.

components.text: Right ventricle myocardium: about 3 to 5 mm

clips.changeMeaning: The right ventricular section is slightly enlarged and labeled with its approximate wall thickness range to highlight its relatively thin myocardium.
clips.narration: The right ventricle usually has a wall thickness of about three to five millimeters. It only needs to pump blood to the lungs, which is a low-pressure circuit.

components.text: Left ventricle myocardium: about 10 to 15 mm

clips.changeMeaning: The left ventricular section is emphasized with its larger thickness range to support direct visual and numerical comparison.
clips.narration: The left ventricle is much thicker, often about ten to fifteen millimeters. It must produce enough pressure to pump blood through the entire systemic circulation.

components.text: Left ventricle is roughly 3 times thicker than right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: A summary ratio label appears to consolidate the anatomical comparison and connect it to functional pressure differences.
clips.narration: A useful summary is that the left ventricular wall is roughly three times thicker than the right ventricular wall because systemic circulation demands far greater pressure.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: Valve states are compared to show how atrioventricular and semilunar valves prevent reverse blood flow during contraction and relaxation.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Classify valves as atrioventricular or semilunar.
Identify which valve group is open or closed during ventricular contraction and relaxation.
Explain how valve closure prevents backflow.
instructions: Advance through the clips to compare valve categories and phases.
Watch how the labels switch between contraction and relaxation.
Relate each valve group to its anatomical location.

clips.changeMeaning: The first clip introduces the atrioventricular valve group and enables a dedicated label for that category.
clips.narration: The tricuspid and mitral valves are atrioventricular valves. They are located between the atria and ventricles.

clips.changeMeaning: The semilunar valve category is added so students can compare it directly with the atrioventricular group.
clips.narration: The pulmonary and aortic valves are semilunar valves. They are located between the ventricles and the arteries leaving the heart.

components.text: Ventricular contraction: AV closed, semilunar open

clips.changeMeaning: The heart is tinted and the phase label updates to illustrate the valve pattern during ventricular contraction.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, the atrioventricular valves are closed to prevent backflow into the atria, while the semilunar valves are open so blood can leave the ventricles.

components.text: Ventricular relaxation: AV open, semilunar closed

clips.changeMeaning: The phase label and heart tint change again to show the opposite valve state during ventricular relaxation and filling.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation, the semilunar valves are closed to prevent blood from returning from the arteries, while the atrioventricular valves open to allow ventricular filling.

modules.description: Students review structure identification in a guided quiz format with visual prompts and narrated feedback.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall names of chambers, valves, and vessels from location cues.
Differentiate among structures using anatomical position.
Use immediate feedback to reinforce correct identification.
instructions: Read the prompt and inspect the heart model.
Use the displayed answer set as a self-check.
Advance to see confirmation and additional quiz guidance.

components.text: A. Right atrium   B. Aorta   C. Mitral valve
Choose the best answer before advancing.

clips.changeMeaning: The guided lab shifts into retrieval practice by presenting an unlabeled structure prompt with answer choices.
clips.narration: Now test your recognition of cardiac structures. Each prompt asks you to identify a highlighted chamber, valve, or vessel from a short set of options.

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback is revealed and the heart model is tinted to mark successful identification and reinforce the answer.
clips.narration: The correct answer is the right atrium, the chamber that receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body.

components.text: More examples: left ventricle, tricuspid valve, pulmonary veins, aorta

clips.changeMeaning: The answer choices are replaced with representative future examples to show the breadth of structures included in the quiz.
clips.narration: A full quiz cycle includes all four chambers, all four valves, and the major vessels. Repeating the quiz helps build fast visual recognition.

modules.description: Students review circulation sequence by identifying the next step in the blood flow pathway and confronting common misconceptions.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall the next structure in blood flow from a given starting point.
Differentiate pulmonary arteries from pulmonary veins by direction of flow and oxygenation state.
Strengthen ordered understanding of the full circulation pathway.
instructions: Read the current blood location prompt.
Predict the next structure before advancing.
Use the reminder about pulmonary arteries and veins to avoid common errors.

components.text: A unit of blood has just entered the right atrium. What comes next?
A. Right ventricle   B. Pulmonary veins   C. Aorta
Flow quiz: identify the next structure in sequence

clips.changeMeaning: The recap of circulation becomes an active sequencing quiz centered on predicting the next correct anatomical step.
clips.narration: This quiz tests whether you can trace blood flow in order. You will be given a current location and asked what structure comes next.

components.text: Correct: blood passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: The sample question is resolved by moving the blood cell to the right ventricle and updating the prompt with the correct explanation.
clips.narration: From the right atrium, blood moves through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle. Thinking step by step helps you avoid sequence errors.

components.text: Reminder: arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood toward it.

clips.changeMeaning: The scene ends with a cautionary reminder about vessel naming, emphasizing a common confusion point in the pulmonary circuit.
clips.narration: A common mistake is mixing up pulmonary arteries and pulmonary veins. Even in the pulmonary circuit, arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood toward the heart.

modules.description: A summary scene reviews the five major concept areas of the lab and reinforces the connections among structure, flow, and function.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Summarize the major structures of the heart.
Integrate blood flow, dual circulation, ventricular asymmetry, and valve function into one conceptual framework.
Prepare for transfer of this knowledge to later cardiovascular physiology topics.
instructions: Advance through the recap items in order.
Use the summary to review before leaving the lab.
Replay earlier scenes if you want more practice on any concept.

components.text: 4. Left vs right ventricular wall thickness

clips.changeMeaning: The summary begins by highlighting the first concept area to orient the learner to a structured recap of the lab.
clips.narration: To conclude, let's review the five key ideas from this heart anatomy lab.

clips.changeMeaning: The first three recap items are highlighted together to connect anatomical inventory with dual circulation and ordered blood flow.
clips.narration: You identified the chambers, valves, and major vessels; distinguished pulmonary and systemic circulation; and traced the full path of blood through both loops.

clips.changeMeaning: The final two recap items are highlighted to reinforce the relationship between ventricular wall thickness and valve-controlled one-way flow.
clips.narration: You also learned why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right and how cardiac valves prevent backflow. Together, these ideas connect heart structure directly to function.
